metadata.note: Yeniden yazildi. Onceki surum 'Technology' adiyla 35 yazilim muhendisligi sorusu tasiyordu ve software_engineering bankasiyla ayni isi anlatiyordu; overlay paketi ise IT destegiydi, yani banka ile paket farkli mesleklerden bahsediyordu. Bu surum paketle hizali: sorun giderme metodu, DNS ve DHCP, dizin hizmeti ve grup politikasi, cihaz yonetimi ve dagitim halkalari, erisim ve gorevden ayrilma, yedek ve geri yukleme testi, ag ve kablosuz, gunluk guvenlik ve kimlik avi mudahalesi, bilet ve dokumantasyon, degisim yonetimi, butce ve ekip.

questions.text: Tell me about yourself and your IT support background.

key_points: Say which layer you work at: end user support, systems and servers, network, identity and access, or IT operations management
Environment in numbers: users supported, sites, ticket volume per week, the device fleet, and users per technician
Stack once: Active Directory or Entra, Intune or Jamf, Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, the ticketing tool, the remote tool
Certifications, since they still screen on these: CompTIA A+ and Network+, Microsoft, Cisco, ITIL
One outcome: resolution time cut, a rollout delivered, onboarding automated, a recurring fault eliminated
Say whether you have worked in a small team where you are the whole department, since that is a different job
strong_answer_signals: Users per technician stated without being asked
Names systems rather than saying computer literate
Says which layer they actually work at
avoid: Describing yourself as good with computers
Vague about which systems you can administer
No ticket volume or user count

questions.text: Tell me about a difficult problem you solved.

key_points: Pick something with a real diagnosis, not a password reset: an intermittent network fault, a failing update, a permissions problem nobody could reproduce, a performance issue
Say how you scoped it first: one user, one machine, one site, or everyone. That single answer changes the whole investigation
Action: what you ruled out and in what order, and what evidence you used rather than guessing
Say when you escalated or called the vendor, and what you handed over
Result: fixed, and whether you found the cause or only the workaround. Be honest about the difference
What you documented so the next person is faster
avoid: Reimaging as the first move
Changing several things at once
A story with no documentation at the end

questions.text: Tell me about a frustrated user you dealt with.

key_points: Acknowledge the impact before the technology. They are not angry about DNS, they are angry about missing a meeting
Action: set expectations honestly, including when you do not yet know. Silence is what turns frustration into escalation
Give a workaround while the real fix runs: a hotspot, a loaner, a shared machine, a phone
Explain without jargon and without condescension. Never say it is user error, even when it is
Follow up after it is fixed, since that one message changes how the department sees IT
Result: the issue resolved and the relationship afterwards
avoid: Blaming the user, even gently
Going silent while working on it
Treating an executive differently on security

questions.text: Tell me about a time you were overwhelmed by tickets.

key_points: Set the volume honestly: a major outage, a rollout gone wrong, a colleague absent, a Monday after a change window
Action: triage by impact times urgency rather than by arrival order
Communicate on the tickets you are NOT working on yet. An unanswered ticket costs more goodwill than a slow one
Escalate early and ask for help rather than quietly drowning
Look for the pattern: twenty tickets about one thing is a project, not twenty tickets
Result: the queue handled and what you changed so it did not repeat
strong_answer_signals: Answers tickets they cannot start yet
Spots the pattern behind the volume
avoid: Working strictly first in first out
Silently absorbing an impossible queue
No follow up on the underlying cause

questions.text: Tell me about a mistake you made.

key_points: Real examples: a change that broke something, a wrong group policy, a deleted account, a misconfigured firewall rule, an update pushed too widely
Own it immediately and tell whoever was affected. In IT a hidden change is far worse than the change
Action: rolled back, contained the impact, and communicated to users before they discovered it
Result and the process you changed: a test group, a change window, a peer review, a backup check first
Say plainly that change control exists because of exactly this
strong_answer_signals: Names the process change, not just the fix
avoid: Saying you have never broken anything
Rolling back quietly and saying nothing
Blaming the vendor or the update

questions.text: Tell me about a project or rollout you delivered.

key_points: Pick something with scope: an operating system upgrade, a mail migration, an identity move, a device refresh, a new ticketing system
Numbers up front: how many users, how many devices, over what window, with what budget
Planning: the pilot group, the rollback plan, the maintenance window, and who you told before you started
Communication is most of the work. What users heard, when, and what you did for those who could not be interrupted
What went wrong, because something did, and how you kept the schedule
Result and what you would do differently
strong_answer_signals: Pilot group and rollback plan both named
avoid: A rollout with no pilot
No rollback position
Users finding out on the day

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to say no to a user request.

key_points: Common ones: local admin rights, personal software, an unapproved cloud service, data on a personal device, bypassing multi factor authentication
Action: understand what they were actually trying to do, since there is usually a safe way to achieve it
Explain the risk in their terms rather than quoting policy at them
Offer the compliant alternative. Being the department of no is how shadow IT starts
Escalate the genuine business case rather than blocking it permanently
Result: the safe route they took, or the exception properly approved and recorded
strong_answer_signals: Finds the safe way to achieve the goal
Escalates a real business case rather than blocking
avoid: Granting local admin to stop the complaints
Quoting policy with no alternative
A flat no that produced shadow IT

questions.text: Tell me about working with a colleague or another team.

key_points: Examples: a developer needing access, facilities during an office move, HR on onboarding, a vendor engineer, security on an incident
Action: understood their constraint before pushing yours, and agreed who does what by when
Say how you handled a disagreement about priority or approach
Result: the outcome and the working relationship afterwards
IT sits between every department. Show that you are easy to work with, since that is half the job
strong_answer_signals: Understands the other side constraint first
avoid: A story where the other team was the obstacle
Handling a disagreement by escalating first
Ignoring a request because it was not logged properly

questions.text: Tell me about feedback you received.

key_points: Real feedback here: ticket notes too thin, slow to update users, not escalating early enough, too much jargon, closing tickets without confirming the fix
Action: asked what good looked like and what you practised
Result: the observable change, ideally in a number such as reopened tickets or first response time
Say whether you asked for a review of your ticket notes afterwards
avoid: Feedback that was really praise
Disagreeing with the standard
No evidence it stuck

questions.text: Tell me about a time you improved something without being asked.

key_points: Options: a knowledge base article, an automated onboarding step, a script for a repeated task, a monitoring alert, a cleaned up asset register
Say what triggered it: usually a task you did three times and got tired of
Action: what you built, who you checked with, and how you got others to use it
Result with a number: hours saved per month, tickets avoided, onboarding time cut
Say how you documented it so it did not become a thing only you understand
strong_answer_signals: Documented so it is not personal knowledge
avoid: A script only you can run or maintain
An improvement nobody else adopted
Automating something without telling anyone

questions.text: Walk me through how you troubleshoot a problem.

key_points: Show a method, because the method IS the question: reproduce, isolate, test one change at a time, verify with the user, document
Define the problem precisely first: what exactly happens, when did it start, what changed, who else is affected
Scope it early: one user, one machine, one site, or everyone. That answer changes the entire investigation
Work the layers in order rather than guessing: physical, network, authentication, application, permissions, data
Say when you escalate and what you hand over: what you tried, what you ruled out, what the logs said
Close the loop with the user in plain language and record the fix
strong_answer_signals: Hands over what was ruled out, not just the symptom
avoid: Reimaging first
Changing several settings at once and hoping
Closing a ticket without confirming with the user

questions.text: Explain DNS and how you troubleshoot it.

key_points: Definition first: DNS resolves a name to an address. Then say the practical truth, that a surprising share of outages are DNS
Know the record types you actually meet: A, CNAME, MX, TXT for verification and mail security, and SRV for some services
Troubleshooting order: is it this machine only, does it resolve with a different resolver, is it cached, is the record correct at the authoritative server
Name the tools: nslookup or dig, ipconfig flushdns, and checking the resolver the client is actually using
Common causes: a stale cache, a wrong or missing record, a client pointing at the wrong DNS server, a TTL that has not expired yet, split horizon differences
Say what you check first when a single site fails versus when everything fails
strong_answer_signals: Knows to test with a different resolver
Names the tools and uses them in a sensible order
avoid: Reciting record types with no troubleshooting method
Flushing DNS as the only technique
Not knowing which resolver the client is using

questions.text: Explain DHCP and what goes wrong with it.

key_points: Definition: automatic address assignment, with the lease process being discover, offer, request, acknowledge
Know the scope: the address range, the lease duration, the reservations, and the options handed out such as gateway and DNS
Real world failures: scope exhaustion, a rogue DHCP server, a failed relay across subnets, a client stuck on an old lease
Symptom recognition: an address in the automatic private range means the client got no answer from a server
Troubleshooting: check the scope utilisation, check the relay, check for a second server, release and renew on the client
Say why reservations matter for printers and infrastructure
strong_answer_signals: Recognises the automatic private address as a no server symptom
Knows about rogue DHCP and relays
avoid: Knowing the acronym but not the failure modes
Release and renew as the whole answer
Not knowing what a relay does

questions.text: What do you know about Active Directory or Entra ID?

key_points: Purpose: identity, authentication and authorisation, with objects organised into containers so policy can be applied by group
Structure: users, groups, computers, organisational units, and why nesting groups by role beats assigning permissions individually
Group policy or its cloud equivalent: settings applied by container, with precedence and inheritance. Say how you troubleshoot a policy that did not apply
Authentication basics: what happens when a user signs in, and the common failures such as time skew, a locked account, a stale cached credential
Hybrid identity: synchronisation between on premises and cloud, and what breaks when sync fails
Say how you handle a joiner, a mover and a leaver, since the mover is the one everyone forgets
strong_answer_signals: Assigns permissions by group, not by user
Can troubleshoot policy that did not apply
Names the mover as the forgotten case
avoid: Assigning permissions to individual users
Not knowing how to check applied policy
No process for role changes

questions.text: How do you manage devices and deployment?

key_points: Standardise the build: a single image or a configuration profile, so machines are alike and support is predictable
Use the management platform properly: enrolment, configuration profiles, compliance policies, application deployment, and remote wipe
Patch on a schedule with a pilot ring first. Pushing an update to everyone at once is how you take out a company
Encryption enabled and the recovery key escrowed centrally, since an encrypted machine with a lost key is a lost machine
Asset records that are accurate: who has what, warranty status, and where it is. Most organisations get this wrong
Have a plan for a lost or stolen device and for a departing employee returning theirs
strong_answer_signals: Asset records treated as a real control
avoid: Pushing updates to everyone at once
Encryption without key escrow
An asset register nobody has verified

questions.text: How do you handle access and permissions?

key_points: Least privilege by default, granted by role rather than by request, and reviewed periodically
Joiners, movers and leavers as a single process. The mover accumulates permissions silently and nobody notices
Offboarding is same day and complete: accounts, mailbox, devices, SaaS applications, shared credentials, building access
Privileged accounts separate from daily accounts, and never shared. Shared admin logins destroy accountability
Multi factor authentication wherever it is possible, and know your exception process
Record who approved each grant, since access without an approver is an audit finding
avoid: Shared admin accounts
Access granted verbally with no record
Offboarding that takes a week

questions.text: How do you approach backups and recovery?

key_points: State the principle: a backup that has never been restored is not a backup, it is a hope
Know the three two one idea: multiple copies, more than one medium, at least one off site or otherwise isolated
Immutable or offline copies matter now, because ransomware targets the backups first
Know the two numbers that define the requirement: how much data you can afford to lose, and how long you can be down
Test restores on a schedule and document the result. Test the full restore, not just a single file
Cloud services still need backup. Retention in a mail platform is not the same as a backup
strong_answer_signals: Says an untested backup is not a backup
Understands cloud services still need backup
avoid: Assuming a backup job that reports success is working
No isolated or immutable copy
Never having done a full restore test

questions.text: What networking do you understand?

key_points: Addressing: what a subnet is, why a device with the wrong mask cannot reach the gateway, and what a default gateway does
The path a packet takes, and how you follow it: check the local machine, the switch port, the VLAN, the gateway, the firewall, then the destination
Tools you actually use: ping, traceroute, nslookup or dig, port testing, and reading the interface status
VLANs and why they exist: segmentation for security and for broadcast control
Wireless problems specifically: coverage versus interference, channel overlap, roaming, and authentication failures. Most wireless complaints are not bandwidth
VPN and remote access: the tunnel, split tunnel or full, certificate or multi factor, and what breaks on a hotel network
strong_answer_signals: Follows the path methodically rather than guessing
Knows most wireless complaints are not bandwidth
Can explain a subnet mask failure
avoid: Rebooting the switch as a diagnostic
Treating every wireless issue as bandwidth
Not knowing how to test a port

questions.text: How do you handle security in day to day IT?

key_points: Patching and endpoint protection on a schedule you can prove, not when someone remembers
Phishing: how a report reaches you, how you contain it, and what you do about the credentials that may already be gone
Multi factor everywhere possible, and treat a multi factor fatigue attack as a real pattern rather than a user error
Least privilege, no shared accounts, and privileged access separated
Know your incident escalation path before you need it, and preserve evidence rather than cleaning up first
Say no to the unsafe request politely and offer the safe version. That skill is why experienced people get hired
Awareness training matters, but design the system so a single mistake is not fatal
strong_answer_signals: Preserves evidence rather than cleaning up
Knows the escalation path in advance
Designs so one mistake is not fatal
avoid: Wiping a compromised machine before anyone investigates
Treating phishing as purely a user training problem
Local admin granted to reduce complaints

questions.text: How do you use ticketing and documentation?

key_points: Log everything, including the walk up requests. Unlogged work is invisible when staffing is discussed
Write ticket notes for the next person, not for yourself: symptom, what you checked, what you ruled out, what fixed it
Categorise honestly so the data can find patterns. Miscategorised tickets make problem management impossible
Know the difference between an incident and a problem: the incident restores service, the problem removes the cause
Build the knowledge base from real tickets, and link the article from the ticket so it gets used
Confirm with the user before closing, since a reopened ticket is worse than an open one
strong_answer_signals: Logs walk ups so the workload is visible
avoid: Fixing at the desk and never logging it
Ticket notes that say fixed
Closing without user confirmation

questions.text: What scripting or automation have you done?

key_points: Be honest about level. Many good technicians are not scripters and employers would rather know
Name the language and what you actually automated: user creation, onboarding steps, reporting, software deployment, log collection, health checks
Say how you tested it before running it widely, since a bad script scales a mistake instantly
Version and document it so it is not personal knowledge that leaves with you
Say what you would automate first here: usually the task the team does most often by hand
Know when not to automate: a rare task, or one where being wrong is expensive
avoid: A script that only runs on your machine
Running an untested script against production
Overstating scripting ability

questions.text: How is IT support measured?

key_points: First response and resolution time against the agreed service levels, split by priority
First contact resolution, which tells you whether the front line is genuinely fixing things
Reopened tickets, which is the honest quality measure and the one most teams ignore
Ticket volume by category, since the pattern points at the problem worth fixing permanently
User satisfaction, taken with care because response rates are low and skewed
Say which you personally influenced and how, with a number
strong_answer_signals: Names reopened tickets as the quality measure
Uses category volume to find root causes
avoid: Closing tickets fast as the only goal
No awareness of service levels
Gaming a metric such as closing and reopening

questions.text: A senior executive says their laptop is broken minutes before a board meeting.

key_points: Get them working first. The meeting is the deliverable, the laptop is not
Fastest path to a working setup: a loaner, a phone or tablet for the call, someone else machine, or dialling in by phone
Then diagnose properly afterwards rather than under pressure in front of an audience
Communicate a clear time: I will have you in the meeting in five minutes, and then meet it
Do not skip security for speed. No shared logins, no disabled encryption, no local admin as a shortcut
Follow up afterwards with the real fix and the cause
strong_answer_signals: Gives a specific time and meets it
Refuses to trade security for speed
avoid: Debugging on the spot while the meeting starts
Handing over a shared or admin login
No follow up on the actual fault

questions.text: A user reports a phishing email they already clicked.

key_points: Thank them first and mean it. A user who reports is worth more than one who hides it, and how you react determines whether the next person reports
Contain immediately: reset the credentials, revoke active sessions and tokens, and check multi factor registrations for anything the attacker added
Check for mail rules created on the account, since forwarding and hiding rules are the classic follow up
Isolate the device if anything was downloaded or run
Search whether the same message reached others and remove it from mailboxes
Report through the incident process. Do not decide alone that it was minor
Preserve evidence rather than cleaning up first
strong_answer_signals: Thanks the reporter, protecting future reporting
Revokes sessions and checks new mail rules
avoid: Making the user feel stupid
Only resetting the password and stopping there
Deciding alone that it was not serious

questions.text: A change you made broke something for many users.

key_points: Roll back first if you can. Understanding can wait, service cannot
Communicate immediately and broadly: what is affected, what you are doing, and when you will update again. Then meet that update time
Own it plainly. Trying to work out whether anyone will notice is the wrong instinct
Once service is restored, find the actual cause rather than assuming
Change the process: a test group, a change window, a peer review, a documented rollback plan
Write it up honestly. A blameless record is what stops it recurring
strong_answer_signals: Changes the process, not just the setting
avoid: Trying to fix it quietly before anyone notices
Restoring service and never finding the cause
No rollback plan existed

questions.text: A user asks for local admin rights to install something.

key_points: Find out what they actually need to do. There is usually a supported way to achieve it
Offer the alternatives: deploy it through the management platform, a portal self service install, a licensed approved equivalent, or a temporary elevation with an expiry
Explain the risk in their terms: one wrong install with admin rights can reach every file they can reach
If there is a genuine business need, take it through the exception process with an approver, a scope and a review date. Do not grant it informally
Record the decision either way
Say plainly that permanent local admin as a convenience is how most endpoint compromises spread
strong_answer_signals: Uses a time limited exception with an approver
avoid: Granting it because they are senior
Refusing with no alternative, producing shadow IT
An informal grant with no record or expiry

questions.text: Several users report the network is slow.

key_points: Scope it first: which users, which sites, which applications, wired or wireless, and when it started
Slow is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Get one concrete measurement before touching anything
Check the obvious in order: is it one application or everything, is it internet or internal, is there a change or an outage upstream
Look at the monitoring rather than the anecdotes. If there is no monitoring, that is your finding
Wireless complaints are usually coverage, interference or client roaming rather than bandwidth
Communicate what you know while you investigate, and give an update time
Afterwards, add the monitoring or alert that would have told you first
strong_answer_signals: Separates internal from internet, one app from all
avoid: Rebooting infrastructure to see what happens
Accepting slow as a diagnosis
No communication while investigating

questions.text: You are asked to give someone access to another person mailbox or files.

key_points: Do not act on the request alone. Verify who is asking and whether they have the authority
Know the proper route: manager approval, HR involvement where it concerns an individual, and a record of the approval
For a departed employee, follow the offboarding process. For someone absent, use a delegated access method rather than sharing their credentials
Never share the person password or log in as them. Use the supported delegation, which also preserves the audit trail
Consider whether legal or HR needs to be involved, particularly in an investigation or a dispute
Record what was granted, to whom, by whose approval, and remove it when it is no longer needed
avoid: Logging in as the user
Granting because a manager asked verbally
Access granted and never removed

questions.text: A critical server or service goes down.

key_points: Confirm the scope and the impact before acting: what is down, who is affected, and what depends on it
Communicate immediately with an update time, and keep the updates coming even when there is no news
Restore service first. Root cause can wait unless the cause is actively making it worse
Work the evidence: monitoring, logs, recent changes. Recent changes are the first place to look and the most commonly skipped
Escalate early to the vendor or the specialist rather than at hour three
Afterwards: root cause, a written record, and the monitoring or redundancy that would have reduced the impact
avoid: Investigating root cause while users are down
Silence during the outage
No post incident review

questions.text: You suspect a machine is infected with malware or ransomware.

key_points: Isolate it from the network immediately, but do not power it off, since memory evidence is lost and some ransomware behaves worse on reboot
Do not start cleaning. Preserve the state for whoever investigates
Escalate through the security incident process at once. This is not a desktop support decision
Check the blast radius: what shares that machine could reach, what credentials were on it, and whether anything else shows the same signs
Check the backups are intact and isolated, since that is what the attacker will have targeted
Communicate carefully and follow the organisation direction on who is told what
Never pay or negotiate. That is a leadership and legal decision, not yours
avoid: Running a cleaner and declaring it fixed
Powering off immediately
Handling it alone as a desktop issue

questions.text: You are the only IT person and three urgent things happen at once.

key_points: Rank by business impact: how many people are stopped, is revenue affected, is there a safety or security dimension
Tell all three what is happening and when you will get to them. Being told you are third is far better than silence
Look for the quick containment on the others: a workaround, a manual process, a temporary access
Ask for help: a colleague, a vendor support line, a managed service contact, or a manager to handle communications
Do not attempt all three in parallel. Context switching under pressure is how mistakes get made
Afterwards, raise the single point of failure honestly, because being the only IT person IS the risk
strong_answer_signals: Ranks by business impact and says so
Raises the single person risk afterwards
avoid: Working all three at once
Silence to the two waiting
Never raising the resourcing risk

questions.text: A user keeps having the same problem every week.

key_points: Stop treating it as an incident and treat it as a problem. Repeatedly restoring service is a failure to fix anything
Gather the pattern: when, after what, on which machine, following which action. Ask the user what they were doing each time
Look at the ticket history properly rather than starting from scratch each week
Test a hypothesis rather than swapping parts. Swapping until it stops is expensive and often coincidental
Consider the causes people skip: a scheduled task, a profile issue, a failing component, a network condition, or a workflow that does not fit the tool
Fix the cause, then confirm over a period rather than declaring victory the same day
Document it, since a recurring fault usually affects more people than the one who reports it
strong_answer_signals: Reframes it as a problem, not an incident
Tests a hypothesis rather than swapping parts
avoid: Applying the same workaround weekly
Replacing hardware without evidence
Closing it the same day and calling it fixed

questions.text: How do you run an IT support team?

key_points: Make the work visible: a queue everyone can see, clear ownership, and service levels that are actually agreed with the business rather than invented
Set standards that are observable: response times, note quality, confirm before closing, escalate at a defined point
Protect project time. A team that is entirely reactive never fixes the cause of anything
Coach on the tickets: review notes, listen to how people talk to users, and give feedback the same week
Balance the load and rotate the unpopular work rather than letting it land on the most agreeable person
Watch the pattern data and turn recurring incidents into projects
avoid: Managing purely from the ticket count
A team that is entirely reactive
Standards that were never agreed with the business

questions.text: How do you handle change management?

key_points: Classify changes: standard and pre approved, normal with review, and emergency with retrospective approval. Without that split, either everything is bureaucratic or nothing is controlled
Every change needs a stated impact, a test, a rollback plan, and a communication step. A change with no rollback is not approved
Schedule windows and respect them, and know the business calendar so you do not change during month end or a peak trading week
Review changes as a group where the risk warrants it, and keep the record
Track change related incidents. If most of your outages follow changes, the process is not working
Make the emergency route real, since a process that cannot handle urgency gets bypassed entirely
strong_answer_signals: Splits standard from normal from emergency
avoid: A process so heavy it gets bypassed
No rollback requirement
Changing during a business peak

questions.text: How do you plan and defend an IT budget?

key_points: Know the run cost first: licences, hardware refresh, support contracts, connectivity, and cloud consumption
Refresh on a cycle rather than on failure. Emergency replacement always costs more and it costs it at the worst time
Justify in business terms: downtime avoided, hours saved, risk reduced, compliance required. Not the specification of the device
Review licences and contracts before renewal. Unused licences and auto renewals are the most common waste
Separate what is genuinely required from what is desirable, and be honest about the consequence of deferring each
Give a number: cost reduced, a contract renegotiated, a consolidation delivered
strong_answer_signals: Knows the run cost before asking for anything new
avoid: Asking for budget in technical specifications
Replacing hardware only on failure
Licences nobody has audited

questions.text: How do you decide what to outsource or buy versus build?

key_points: Start from what is core: things that differentiate the business stay close, commodity services can be bought
Count the real cost of building: the build, the run, the on call, the documentation, and the person who owns it in three years
Consider the risk of the single person who knows how it works. That is the most common hidden cost in small IT teams
For a managed service: define what good looks like in the contract, keep the ability to leave, and retain enough knowledge to hold them to account
Do not outsource the accountability. The vendor can run it, you still own the outcome
Review the arrangement periodically rather than renewing by habit
strong_answer_signals: Counts run cost and key person risk
Retains enough knowledge to hold a vendor to account
avoid: Building something that becomes one person knowledge
Outsourcing and assuming accountability transfers
Renewing a managed service without review

questions.text: How do you improve service without more headcount?

key_points: Attack the top ticket categories. A small number of causes usually generates most of the volume
Self service for the repeatable: password reset, software install, access request, and a knowledge base people can actually find
Automate onboarding and offboarding, which are high volume, error prone and security relevant
Fix the underlying causes rather than getting faster at the same repairs
Shift left: give the front line the tools and permissions to resolve rather than escalating everything
Measure before and after, and be honest when something did not work
Give the number: volume reduced, first contact resolution improved, onboarding time cut
strong_answer_signals: Targets the top categories rather than working faster
Shifts resolution to the front line
avoid: Asking people to work harder
A knowledge base nobody can find
Measuring speed while volume grows

questions.text: How do you manage security risk as an IT manager?

key_points: Know your actual exposure: what data you hold, where it is, who can reach it, and what would hurt most if lost
Get the basics right before buying tools: patching, multi factor, least privilege, backup with an isolated copy, and endpoint protection
Have an incident response plan people have rehearsed, and know who decides and who communicates
Manage third party risk. Your suppliers access is your exposure
Report risk to leadership in business terms with options and costs, and record when a risk is accepted rather than fixed
Never present a security posture as complete. Present it as a position with known gaps and a plan
avoid: Buying a product instead of fixing patching and access
A plan nobody has rehearsed
Claiming the environment is secure

questions.text: How do you keep and develop IT staff?

key_points: Know why people leave IT roles: no progression, permanently reactive work, no training budget, being blamed for systems they did not choose, and on call with no recognition
Give project work and time to do it, since that is where people learn and stay
Fund certification and give study time. It is cheaper than replacing someone
Rotate specialisms so nobody is trapped as the only person who knows a system, which helps them and reduces your risk
Recognise the invisible work. IT is noticed when it fails and ignored when it works
Manage the on call load fairly and pay or compensate it properly
Give the number: turnover or average tenure
strong_answer_signals: Names permanently reactive work as a retention issue
Rotates specialisms to remove key person risk
avoid: Training budget as the first thing cut
One person owning a critical system indefinitely
On call treated as goodwill

questions.text: How do you work with the rest of the business?

key_points: Be present before you are needed. A manager who only appears when something breaks is treated as a cost centre
Translate: talk about downtime, risk, hours and cost rather than about the technology
Get involved early in projects. IT invited at the end inherits decisions it cannot fix
Say yes to the objective and negotiate the method. A flat no drives shadow IT and you find out later
Report honestly, including the things that are going badly, and bring options rather than only problems
Build a relationship with the people who set budgets before you need one
strong_answer_signals: Says yes to the objective, negotiates the method
avoid: Appearing only during incidents
Blocking requests without alternatives
Being invited to projects at the end and accepting that

questions.text: Why do you want to work in IT support?

key_points: Give a real reason: you like solving problems, you like that the work has an obvious result, you enjoy helping people who are stuck
Connect it to something you actually did, including outside work
Say what you want to grow into: systems, network, security, cloud, or team lead
Practical reasons such as stability and a clear certification path are respected when paired with genuine interest
strong_answer_signals: A concrete reason tied to real experience
Names a direction they want to grow in
avoid: Saying you are good with computers
Nothing about the people you would be helping
Treating support as a stepping stone with no interest in it

questions.text: Why this organisation?

key_points: Be specific: the size, the sector, whether they are cloud first, regulated, growing, or mid migration
Connect it to your experience: a similar environment, a system they use, a transition you have done before
Say what you want to learn there and what you could bring in the first months
Be honest about practical fit alongside the real reason
strong_answer_signals: Connects their experience to the context
Says what they would bring early
avoid: An answer that fits any employer
Getting the size or the sector wrong
Only mentioning location or salary

questions.text: How do you keep your skills current?

key_points: Name the actual sources: vendor documentation, certification study, home lab, communities, release notes, and the vendors you already use
Say what you have learned recently and where it showed up in your work. That is the evidence, not the intention
A home lab or a personal project is genuinely persuasive in this field. Say what you built and why
Say how you evaluate something new rather than adopting it because it is popular
Mention the direction of the field honestly: cloud, identity, automation and security are where the work is moving
strong_answer_signals: Names something learned recently and where it was used
A home lab or real project
avoid: Saying you keep up with no example
Only listing certifications you intend to take
No awareness of where the field is moving

questions.text: How do you handle repetitive work?

key_points: Be honest. A share of this job is repetitive and pretending otherwise is not credible
Say how you handle it: do it well and consistently, then look for what can be automated or self served
Say that the repetitive ticket is often someone bad day, so consistency matters to them even when it is routine to you
Give an example of something repetitive you removed or reduced
Say what balance you want: some routine, some project work, and be honest that entirely reactive roles wear people down
strong_answer_signals: Honest that some of it is routine
Knows the routine ticket matters to the user
avoid: Claiming to love repetition
Suggesting routine work is beneath you
No example of improving anything

questions.text: Where do you want to be in a couple of years?

key_points: Honest options: senior support, systems or network administration, security, cloud, identity, or team lead
If you want to stay at the front line and be excellent at it, say so. Experienced reliable support staff are valued and increasingly rare
Name what you would need: a certification, exposure to a specific system, or project experience
Show you intend to do this job well regardless of the direction
strong_answer_signals: Names a direction and what it requires
Comfortable saying they want to stay hands on
Committed to the current role regardless
avoid: Claiming ambitions you do not have
No thought about direction
Making clear you will leave as soon as possible

questions.text: Do you have any questions for us?

key_points: Ask what tells you what the job actually is:
"How many users per technician, and what is the ticket volume?"
"Is the team firefighting, or is there protected project time?"
"What is the state of documentation and the asset register?"
"Who decides on tooling and budget?"
"What is the biggest thing you know needs fixing?"
The firefighting versus project split is the most honest description of the role you will get
strong_answer_signals: Asks about the firefighting versus project split
Asks what they know needs fixing
avoid: No questions
Only asking about pay and hours
Asking something already in the advert
